data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Centralized services with high redundancy are actually more resilient because they can implement 'Synthetic Diversity' and coordinated recovery, whereas decentralized networks suffer from 'stochastic synchronization' via shared external triggers.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The central control plane itself becomes the single point of failure (SPOF).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The 'Herding Effect' (ref: SCR_002) causes redundant nodes to synchronize their failure (e.g., retry storms) in a way that a messy, decentralized network would avoid.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Coordinated Mitigation: A large service can intentionally run diverse versions of its own software (ref: SCR_004) and use a global control plane to detect and isolate a failing version instantly. Decentralized networks lack this global visibility, meaning a correlated failure (e.g., a Leap Second bug, ref: SCR_001) propagates blindly across the network without a central mechanism to 'brake' the failure.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
